source.title: Can Stability be Detrimental? Better Generalization through Gradient Descent Instabilities

record.tranche_reason: The study trains randomly initialized networks with gradient descent and reports training completion, learning-rate stability behavior, and generalization outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cited prior work on edge-of-stability training and generalization; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Learning rates used to select settings are also not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures training loss and Hessian sharpness during full-batch gradient descent, including instability above 2/η and recovery, as in V5's edge-of-stability experiments. Its CIFAR-10 training-completion results also bear on V1 using full-batch GD rather than SGD or Adam.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors argue that large-rate full-batch GD induces eigenvector rotations and progressive flattening associated with improved generalization, and recommend rates above descent-lemma bounds. Recovery through this mechanism remains a conjecture; extremely large rates can diverge, and extension to SGD is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Full-batch gradient descent with cross-entropy in the main CIFAR experiments, GhostBatchNorm, and small VGG/ResNet models; no momentum, RMSProp, weight decay, or common stochastic augmentation in the initial experiments. This paper emphasizes instability, eigenvector rotation, and generalization rather than the specific squared-loss recipes in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and duration above the stability threshold; dataset difficulty; extremely large learning rates can diverge; timing of learning-rate reduction changes validation outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Instabilities rotate Hessian eigenvectors, and reducing the learning rate can reverse those rotations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training stability changes Hessian eigenvector orientation.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation accuracy improves with sufficiently large learning rates, while learning-rate reduction can lower validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large learning rates can improve generalization, with benefits depending on their magnitude and reduction timing.

fits_no_version.finding: Completed fMNIST MLP runs exceed 99.99% training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small MLPs can interpolate a 1,000-example fMNIST training set using full-batch GD.

record.code_released: The paper says code will be made available on GitHub upon publication; no URL stated.
record.problems: The CIFAR-10 experiments in Sections 4.1–4.2 use a 5k subset; full-dataset stability limits were not computed. Numerical validation values for the learning-rate sweeps in Figure 5 are only shown in plots. The paper notes a small sample size for the controlled-initialization correlation analysis and limited evidence overall. Training completion is stated as a criterion, without per-model training accuracy values.
record.rows_left_out: No required results omitted. The paper's correlation analysis between sharpness/eigenvector similarity and generalization does not itself measure the instability behavior named by V5, so it was not included as a row.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD and Adam, and systematic comparisons involving capacity, early stopping, or regularization. The reported CIFAR experiments use full-batch GD.
Teacher–student ReLU local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Matched depth comparisons, degradation with longer training, identity-shortcut controls, and special initialization remedies.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, training speed, and trainable depth.

The wide squared-loss initial-catapult recipe, systematic long-time loss reduction while sharpness hovers at the threshold, and divergence from an explicitly measured initially subthreshold rate. Full-dataset CIFAR stability thresholds were not computed.
Matched normalization versus no-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

missing.what: Separate training-outcome rows for successful above-threshold runs and eventual divergence in the fMNIST and CIFAR10-5k sweeps. Existing rows record validation accuracy rather than these V5 outcomes.
Full-dataset models diverged at η=6.4, whereas η=3.2 remained functional. Record this separately, retaining the caveat that stability thresholds were not computed.
The authors' own MLP trajectory shows sharpness reaching 2/η through progressive sharpening, followed by instability cycles with coincident loss, sharpness, and oscillation peaks.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Uncomputed stability thresholds and worse validation accuracy after rate reduction do not justify limits_scope verdicts on V5. Deliberately choosing a large learning rate is an optimization condition, not an instruction that specifies the resulting recovery behavior.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests training completion on fMNIST and CIFAR-10 with specified small networks. It does not report CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, Adam, or comparisons with smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.

The paper studies full-batch gradient descent with cross-entropy on fMNIST and CIFAR-10, plus a toy model. It does not test the squared-loss wide-network recipe in Lewkowycz et al. or the extended sharpness-hovers-at-threshold behavior in Cohen et al.; CIFAR-10 stability limits were not computed for the full-dataset models.
